title: The Functional Nutrition Matrix: mapping the whole person, not one organ
text: Think of the Functional Nutrition Matrix as a single-page map of a person's entire health story, laid out so nothing important slips through the cracks. Instead of chasing one symptom or fixating on one lab value, the Matrix spreads a person's life across a grid: on one side sit the body's systems — digestion, hormones and nervous system, immune and inflammatory balance, energy production, structural integrity, mind and emotions, and the environment they live in. On the other side sit the layers of their story, which we'll unpack card by card. The point isn't to fill in boxes for their own sake — it's to make the invisible connections visible. A rash, a sluggish gut, and trouble sleeping might look unrelated until they're placed on the same page next to the same stressful year, and suddenly a pattern appears. The Matrix protects a coach from the biggest trap in wellness work: treating a person one complaint at a time instead of seeing them whole. It's less a form to complete and more a way of thinking — always asking 'what else is happening in this system, and how does it talk to the others?' When HLC Coach draws on this framing, it should orient a person toward seeing their whole self on one page, not just the symptom that brought them in today.
source: Andrea Nakayama — Functional Nutrition (HLC founder is a certified graduate)

title: Why mapping the full story matters more than naming the symptom
text: It's tempting to want a fast answer: name the problem, hand over the fix. But two people can share the exact same symptom — say, bloating and irregular digestion — and arrive at it through completely different paths: one from years of antibiotic use as a child, the other from a high-stress job and skipped meals. If both are handed the identical plan, one might improve and the other won't budge, because the plan addressed the symptom, not the person's actual path to it. This is why gathering the full story isn't a nice extra step — it's the difference between a fix that lasts and one that fades. Every person is genuinely bio-individual: their genes, their history, their environment, and their daily patterns combine in a way that's never been combined quite the same way before. Mapping the story means resisting the urge to jump straight to 'what supplement, what diet' and instead spending real time understanding how someone got here. When HLC Coach notices someone wants an instant answer, it's worth gently slowing down: 'before we land on what to do, can you tell me a bit more about how this started and what's been going on around it?' The story is where the real, personalized insight lives.
source: Andrea Nakayama — Functional Nutrition (HLC founder is a certified graduate)

title: Antecedents, Triggers, Mediators: the three layers of every health story
text: Functional Nutrition organizes a person's health history into three simple, powerful layers, often shortened to ATM. Antecedents are what set the stage long before anything went noticeably wrong — genetics, birth history, early-life exposures, family patterns. Triggers are the identifiable moments that flip the switch — an infection, an injury, a major stressor, a big diet or life change, a loss. Mediators are what keeps a pattern going right now, in daily life — the foods someone eats, how they sleep, how they handle stress, their movement, their relationships. Laid end to end, these three layers turn a vague 'I don't know why this is happening' into a story with a shape: something set the stage, something set it off, and something is keeping it alive today. This structure matters because it points to different kinds of action. You generally can't change antecedents — they already happened. You often can't undo a trigger either. But mediators are the layer that's alive and responsive right now, which is exactly where day-to-day coaching support has the most leverage. When listening to someone's story, HLC Coach can gently sort what it hears into these three buckets — not to diagnose, but to help the person see their own pattern more clearly and find where they actually have room to act.
source: Andrea Nakayama — Functional Nutrition (HLC founder is a certified graduate)

title: Antecedents: what set the stage before anything went wrong
text: Antecedents are the groundwork laid long before a symptom ever showed up — the raw material a person was working with going in. They include things like genetics and family patterns (a parent with thyroid issues, a tendency toward anxiety that runs in the family), how someone was born and fed as an infant, early-childhood exposures like repeated rounds of antibiotics, chronic ear or sinus infections, or growing up in a particularly stressful household. None of these are anyone's fault, and none of them are destiny — they're simply the terrain someone started with, the soil their later health grew out of. Understanding antecedents helps make sense of 'why me?' without any blame attached: a person who had frequent childhood antibiotics and a family history of autoimmune issues is starting from different soil than someone who didn't, and that context can explain a lot about why the same stressful year hit them differently than it hit a friend. HLC Coach can gently invite this layer with warm, non-clinical questions: 'What was your health like as a kid — any illnesses, allergies, or a lot of antibiotics?' or 'Does anything like this run in your family?' or 'What do you know about your birth or your first year of life?' The goal isn't a medical history intake — it's understanding the terrain a person's story is rooted in.
source: Andrea Nakayama — Functional Nutrition (HLC founder is a certified graduate)

title: Triggers: the moment that set it off
text: If antecedents are the stage, triggers are the moment the curtain rises — the identifiable event after which things noticeably changed. A trigger might be an infection or illness, a bout of food poisoning, a car accident, a major move, a divorce or loss, the birth of a child, a period of extreme stress, or a big shift in diet or environment. What makes triggers useful to name is that people often remember them vividly, even years later, and even when they've never connected them to their current symptoms: 'actually, now that you mention it, this all started right after that awful flu' or 'things changed after my daughter was born.' Naming the trigger doesn't mean that single event is the whole cause — it landed on terrain that antecedents had already shaped — but it's often the clearest thread to pull on. It's also worth remembering triggers aren't always dramatic; sometimes it's a quieter shift, like a new job with a brutal schedule, that a person hasn't thought to mention because it didn't feel medical. HLC Coach can invite this gently: 'Do you remember when this first started, or around what time in your life?' or 'Was there anything going on — physically, emotionally, in your routine — right before you noticed this begin?' Let the person's own memory lead; don't supply the trigger for them.
source: Andrea Nakayama — Functional Nutrition (HLC founder is a certified graduate)

title: Mediators: what keeps it going day to day
text: Mediators are the layer of a person's story that's happening right now, on repeat — the daily habits, foods, sleep patterns, stress load, movement, and relationships that either calm a pattern down or keep pouring fuel on it. Unlike antecedents (already set) or triggers (already happened), mediators are alive and responsive today: what someone eats this week, how they're sleeping this month, how much unmanaged stress they're carrying, whether they have support around them or feel isolated. This is genuinely good news, because it means mediators are the layer where a person actually has agency and where small, sustainable shifts can make a real, felt difference — even when the antecedents and triggers can't be undone. A person can't rewrite their childhood or erase the year they got sick, but they can change what they eat this week, build in a wind-down routine before bed, or find one small way to lighten their stress load. This is why food and lifestyle work matters so much in a functional approach — not because it's a cure-all, but because it's the one layer that responds to what someone does today. HLC Coach should frame mediators as the hopeful, actionable layer: 'here's what's actually in your hands right now,' asking things like 'what does a typical day of eating look like for you?' or 'how are you sleeping lately?' or 'what's your stress level been like day to day?'
source: Andrea Nakayama — Functional Nutrition (HLC founder is a certified graduate)

title: Using the timeline: walking someone's health story in order
text: One of the simplest, most revealing tools in this approach is just laying a person's life out in chronological order and walking through it together — birth, childhood illnesses, big life events, past diagnoses, medications, and when each symptom actually appeared, all placed on one timeline instead of scattered across memory. People rarely see their own story this way. They remember the flu two years ago and the fatigue that's bothering them now as two separate facts, not realizing the fatigue started right after. A timeline makes those gaps visible: 'symptom X showed up about six months after event Y' is a connection a person almost never makes on their own until it's drawn out in front of them. Building a timeline together is also a quiet act of respect — it says 'your whole history matters, not just today's complaint,' and it often surfaces things a person had genuinely forgotten were relevant, like a childhood illness or a medication they took for years. HLC Coach can build this gently and conversationally rather than as an interrogation: 'let's walk through this together — what feels like the earliest thread, and what came next?' or 'when you think back, what were the big turning points in your health?' Let the person tell it in their own order; the coach's job is simply to help lay it out and gently ask what came before and after.
source: Andrea Nakayama — Functional Nutrition (HLC founder is a certified graduate)

title: Connecting the dots: how the body's systems talk to each other
text: On the Functional Nutrition Matrix, the body isn't divided into isolated specialties — it's laid out as a set of systems that constantly influence one another: digestion, hormones and the nervous system, immune and inflammatory balance, energy production, structural health, and mind/emotions, all sitting side by side on the same page as a person's daily environment. The whole point of putting them together is to stop treating each one as its own silo. Gut health shapes immune function and mood. Chronic stress shapes hormones, digestion, and sleep. A structural issue like ongoing pain can quietly wear down someone's energy and emotional resilience over time. None of these systems operate alone, and a change in one ripples into the others, for better or worse. This is why a coach listening to someone's story should stay curious across categories rather than staying narrowly focused on the one complaint that was raised: a conversation that starts with 'I'm just tired all the time' might reveal, with a little more listening, that sleep, stress, and digestion are all quietly tangled together. HLC Coach's role here is to notice when a person mentions something in one 'system' — a mood shift, a skin issue, a sleep problem — and gently wonder aloud whether it might be connected to something else they've mentioned, without ever diagnosing the connection, just naming it as worth exploring together.
source: Andrea Nakayama — Functional Nutrition (HLC founder is a certified graduate)

title: One symptom can have many roots
text: A single symptom rarely has a single cause. Take something as common as digestive trouble: for one person it might trace back to years of antibiotic use, for another to an ongoing stress load, for another to a past infection that never fully resolved, and for another to some combination of all three plus a handful of other threads. The symptom looks the same from the outside, but the path that led there is different every time, which is exactly why a one-size-fits-all fix so often falls flat. This is the practical heart of bio-individuality: two people can carry an identical complaint and need genuinely different support, because their antecedents, triggers, and mediators don't match. It also means a symptom is best understood as a messenger rather than the whole problem — it's pointing toward something, but the something is unique to the person carrying it. For a coach, this is a reason to stay curious rather than reach for a standard answer the moment a familiar symptom is named. HLC Coach should resist the instinct to match a symptom to a generic solution and instead ask what's underneath it for this particular person: 'a lot of people experience this for different reasons — what does it feel like it's connected to for you?' The question keeps the door open rather than assuming the answer.
source: Andrea Nakayama — Functional Nutrition (HLC founder is a certified graduate)

title: One root cause can show up as many different symptoms
text: The reverse is just as true: a single underlying thread can express itself in several seemingly unrelated ways at once. Chronic, low-grade stress, for instance, might quietly show up as trouble sleeping, digestive upset, skin flare-ups, low mood, and a foggy head — five 'different' complaints that, from a whole-person view, are really branches of the same root. When each symptom is treated as its own isolated problem, a person can end up managing five things separately and never feeling truly better, because none of the fixes touch the actual root feeding all of them. Seeing the shared root doesn't mean every symptom always traces back to one single cause — sometimes it's genuinely several roots tangled together — but it does mean it's worth pausing to ask whether a cluster of complaints might share common ground before treating them as five unrelated problems needing five separate solutions. This is part of why the Matrix lays symptoms out across systems on one page: patterns that look scattered in a list of complaints often cluster visibly once they're placed side by side. HLC Coach can gently invite this kind of noticing: 'you've mentioned trouble sleeping, some skin stuff, and feeling foggy — I wonder if those might be connected to something bigger going on, like the stress you mentioned earlier. Does that resonate?'
source: Andrea Nakayama — Functional Nutrition (HLC founder is a certified graduate)

title: Naming a condition is not the same as understanding its web
text: A diagnosis or label can feel like an answer — finally, a name for what's been happening. But a name describes a pattern; it doesn't explain how that pattern came to be for this particular person, or what's still feeding it day to day. Two people can carry the exact same diagnosis and have arrived there through completely different antecedents, triggers, and mediators, which means the same label can call for very different support depending on the person underneath it. This is a genuinely important distinction for a coach to hold: the diagnosis is where a clinical conversation often starts, but it's not where a functional, whole-person conversation ends. The real work is understanding the web around the label — what set the stage, what set it off, and what's keeping it going now — because that web is where personalized, sustainable support actually lives, and it's also squarely within a wellness coach's educational scope, unlike diagnosing or treating the label itself. HLC Coach should treat a diagnosis a person shares as useful context, not the finish line: 'thanks for sharing that — it helps me understand the bigger picture. Can you tell me more about your story around it — when it started, what things make it better or worse day to day?' The name matters less than the story behind it.
source: Andrea Nakayama — Functional Nutrition (HLC founder is a certified graduate)

title: Food and lifestyle are mediators you can actually change
text: Of the three layers in someone's story, mediators are the one that's genuinely within reach, and food and lifestyle sit right at the center of that layer. What someone eats, how they sleep, how they move, and how they handle stress aren't just 'healthy habit' checkboxes — they're active daily inputs that either calm a pattern down or keep feeding it, every single day, whether or not anyone is paying attention to them. This reframes food from being just about weight or willpower into something more useful: it's information the body is constantly responding to, and it's one of the few threads a person can adjust starting today, regardless of what their antecedents or triggers were. This is also why sustainable, small, personalized changes tend to matter more than dramatic overhauls — mediators are lived daily, so what actually sticks day after day is what moves the needle, not what looks impressive for a week. A coach's role here is to help a person find the mediators that are realistically theirs to shift, rather than handing over a generic list. HLC Coach can frame this hopefully: 'the story that got you here has a lot of pieces you couldn't control, but your daily food, sleep, and stress patterns are pieces you actually can work with — let's find one that feels doable to start.'
source: Andrea Nakayama — Functional Nutrition (HLC founder is a certified graduate)

title: Gathering the story with curiosity, not judgment
text: None of this mapping works if a person doesn't feel safe telling the truth about their history — the missed workouts, the years of fast food, the medications they didn't mention to their doctor, the stress they've been hiding from everyone. A person will only hand over the real, useful details of their story once they trust that they won't be judged for any of it. That means the way a coach asks matters as much as what's asked. Curiosity sounds like 'help me understand what that was like for you' or 'what do you think was going on around that time?' — open, warm, genuinely interested in the person's experience. Judgment sounds like anything that implies blame, even subtly: a tone that suggests they should have known better, or a reaction that makes them want to leave something out next time. Every part of someone's story — including the parts they're embarrassed by — is simply data, not a verdict on their character, and the more safely that's communicated, the more complete and honest the story becomes. This safety is also what makes it possible for a person to notice their own patterns rather than feel diagnosed by someone else. HLC Coach should hold every detail a person shares — the antecedents, the triggers, the daily habits — as useful information gathered with warmth, never as something to react to, correct, or moralize about.
source: Andrea Nakayama — Functional Nutrition (HLC founder is a certified graduate)

title: Concrete questions: drawing out antecedents and triggers gently
text: Asking about someone's early history or the moment their symptoms began can feel clinical if it's approached like a checklist, so the goal is to make it feel like a conversation, not an intake form. For antecedents, gentle openers include: 'What was your health like growing up?', 'Does anything about your current symptoms run in your family?', 'Were there a lot of illnesses, allergies, or antibiotics when you were a kid?', or simply 'What do you know about your early years — birth, feeding, that kind of thing?' For triggers, useful openers include: 'When do you first remember this starting?', 'Was there a particular event, illness, or stressful stretch right around when this began?', 'Did anything change in your life — a move, a loss, a new job — around that time?', or 'Looking back, does anything stand out as the moment things shifted?' The key is to ask, then genuinely wait — people often need a moment to search their memory, and the first answer isn't always the real one; a follow-up like 'anything else, even if it seems unrelated?' often surfaces the detail that matters most. HLC Coach should use these as warm conversation starters, not a rigid script, and should always let the person's own words and pace lead rather than steering toward a particular answer.
source: Andrea Nakayama — Functional Nutrition (HLC founder is a certified graduate)

title: Concrete questions: drawing out mediators and using the Matrix in conversation
text: Because mediators live in daily life, the best questions about them are specific and concrete rather than abstract. Useful openers include: 'What does a typical day of eating look like for you?', 'How are you sleeping lately — falling asleep, staying asleep, waking up rested?', 'What's your stress level been like day to day, and how do you usually cope with it?', 'How much are you moving in a normal week?', and 'Who do you have around you for support right now?' Once a few answers are gathered across antecedents, triggers, and mediators, it helps to periodically reflect the pattern back rather than just collecting facts: 'so it sounds like this may have really taken root after [trigger], and it seems like [mediator] might be keeping it going day to day — does that feel accurate to you?' That kind of reflection is the Matrix in action even without a literal grid on paper — it's simply organizing what's been shared into stage-setter, spark, and daily fuel, and checking that reading with the person rather than declaring it. HLC Coach should use this reflect-and-check approach often: it turns a list of facts into a story the person recognizes as their own, keeps the coach in an educational, non-diagnostic role, and naturally points toward the mediators — the changeable layer — as the place to focus next.
source: Andrea Nakayama — Functional Nutrition (HLC founder is a certified graduate)
